about: The scripted AI lesson for p3-pressure (2026-11-17, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p3-particle-model and p1-energy-stores.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about the pressure a gas makes: what causes it, and how heating or squashing a gas changes it.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. Everything is made of tiny particles. How do the particles in a gas move?

options.text: They slide past each other, touching

steps.right: Yes: gas particles are far apart and move fast in random directions.

wrong.other: Not quite: fast, in random directions.
wrong.vibrate: Not quite: vibrating about fixed places is a solid. Gas particles move fast in random directions.
wrong.slide: Not quite: sliding past each other while touching is a liquid. Gas particles move fast in random directions.

idk.hint: In a solid the particles vibrate in place; in a liquid they slide past each other. Which button is left for a gas?

steps.answerWhy: Gas particles are far apart and move fast in random directions.

steps.question: Second: which energy store is filled by movement?
steps.right: Yes: kinetic, the store for moving things.

wrong.thermal: Not quite: the thermal store is the energy of a hot object. The store filled by movement is the kinetic store.
wrong.chem: Not quite: the chemical store is in fuels and food. Movement fills the kinetic store.

idk.hint: A car has more energy in this store the faster it goes. Which store is that?

steps.text: Now this lesson. Gas particles do not all move at the same speed: at any moment some are fast and some are slow.
A moving particle has kinetic energy: the energy of movement. The faster it moves, the more kinetic energy it has.
A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N).

Gas particles keep hitting each other and the walls of their container. When a particle hits a wall it bounces off. Each hit like this is called a collision, and it pushes on the wall with a tiny force.
Billions of collisions every second add up to a steady push on every part of the wall, at right angles to the wall.
Pressure is the force on each square metre of a surface: pressure = force ÷ area.
With the force in newtons and the area in square metres (m²), the pressure comes out in pascals (Pa). Pressures are often given in kilopascals (kPa): 1 kPa = 1000 Pa.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A force of 100 N pushes evenly on an area of 4 m². What is the pressure?
steps: Write the equation: pressure = force ÷ area.

steps.question: A force of 600 N pushes evenly on an area of 2 m². What is the pressure, in Pa?
steps.right: Yes: 300 Pa. Pressure = force ÷ area = 600 ÷ 2 = 300 Pa.

wrong.other: Not quite: 300 Pa. Pressure = force ÷ area = 600 ÷ 2 = 300 Pa.
wrong.times: Not quite: you multiplied. Pressure = force ÷ area = 600 ÷ 2 = 300 Pa.
wrong.upside: Not quite: you divided the area by the force. Pressure = force ÷ area = 600 ÷ 2 = 300 Pa.

idk.hint: Divide the force, 600, by the area, 2.

steps.text: The push of gas particles colliding with each square metre of their container's walls is called the gas pressure. More collisions each second, or harder collisions, mean a higher pressure.

steps.question: More air is pumped into a box through a valve, then the valve is closed. The temperature stays the same. Which is true of the pressure in the box?
steps.right: Yes: more particles in the same space means more collisions with the walls each second, so the pressure rises.

wrong.falls: Not quite: there are now more particles to hit the walls, so there are more collisions each second: the pressure rises.
wrong.same: Not quite: more particles in the same box hit the walls more often each second, so the pressure rises.

idk.hint: More particles in the box means more collisions with the walls each second. Does that make the pressure rise, fall or stay the same?

steps.answerWhy: More particles means more collisions with the walls each second, so the pressure rises.

steps.text: Still air in a closed room presses on the walls too. Even when the air as a whole is not moving, its particles never stop.

steps.question: A balloon is blown up and tied. Why does it stay round?

options.text: Collisions from inside push out on all the rubber
The rubber pulls itself into a ball
Air fills the gaps in the rubber

steps.right: Yes: collisions push outwards on every part of the rubber, at right angles to it, so it stays round.

wrong.other: Not quite: collisions from inside push out on all the rubber.
wrong.rubber: Not quite: the stretched rubber pulls inwards. It stays round because air particles inside collide with every part of it, pushing outwards.
wrong.gaps: Not quite: the air is inside the balloon. Its particles collide with the rubber, pushing outwards everywhere.

idk.hint: The air inside is a gas. What do its particles keep doing to the walls of their container?

steps.answerWhy: Air particles inside collide with every part of the rubber, pushing outwards at right angles to it.

steps.prompt: In one line: what causes gas pressure?
points: particles colliding with the walls of the container
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: gas pressure is caused by the particles colliding with the walls of their container.

keyPoints.heading: Temperature and pressure at constant volume

steps.text: Keep a gas in a sealed, rigid container, one that cannot bend or stretch. Then its volume, the space it takes up, cannot change: the gas is at constant volume.
The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its particles: the higher the temperature, the faster the particles move on average.

steps.question: A sealed metal can of gas is heated. Predict: which is true of the pressure inside?

options.text: It stays the same, as the volume is fixed

steps.right: Yes: the pressure rises. Next, why.

wrong.other: Not quite: it rises. Next, why.
wrong.fall: Not quite: it rises. Heating makes the particles faster, not slower; why that raises the pressure comes next.
wrong.same: Not quite: the volume is fixed, but the pressure still rises. Next, why.

idk.hint: In a hotter gas the particles move faster, so they hit the walls more often and harder. Does the pressure rise, fall or stay the same?

steps.answerWhy: Heating a gas at constant volume makes its pressure rise.

steps.text: Heated particles move faster. They hit the walls more often each second, and each collision pushes harder, so the pressure rises.
Cooling does the opposite: the particles slow down, so the pressure falls.

steps.question: A sealed can of gas is put in a freezer. Why does the pressure inside fall?

options.text: Slower particles hit the walls less often and less hard
The particles stick to the cold walls
The particles shrink in the cold

steps.right: Yes: cooling slows the particles, so they hit the walls less often each second and less hard.

wrong.other: Not quite: slower particles hit the walls less often and less hard.
wrong.stick: Not quite: the particles keep moving and bouncing. They are slower, so they hit the walls less often and less hard.
wrong.shrink: Not quite: particles never change size. They move more slowly, so they hit the walls less often and less hard.

idk.hint: Cooling slows the particles down. Which option describes slower particles?

steps.answerWhy: Cooling slows the particles, so they hit the walls less often each second and less hard: the pressure falls.

steps.prompt: In one line: why does heating a gas in a sealed, rigid container raise its pressure?
points: they hit the walls more often each second
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the particles move faster, so they hit the walls more often each second and harder, so the pressure rises.

keyPoints.heading: Pressure and volume at constant temperature

steps.text: Now keep the temperature fixed and change the volume instead, like pushing in the plunger of a sealed syringe.
Squashing a gas into a smaller volume is called compressing it. Letting it spread into a bigger volume is letting it expand.

steps.question: A sealed syringe of air is compressed to half its volume, at the same temperature. Predict: which is true of the pressure?

wrong.other: Not quite: it doubles. Next, why.
wrong.halve: Not quite: it doubles. Less space means more collisions with the walls, not fewer; why it doubles comes next.
wrong.same: Not quite: it doubles. The particles have not changed, but their space has; why that matters comes next.

idk.hint: Same particles, same speed, half the space. Think about how often each one reaches a wall.

steps.answerWhy: Compressing a gas into half the volume at the same temperature doubles its pressure.

steps.text: In half the space, the same particles hit each part of the wall twice as often each second. Their speed has not changed, because the temperature has not.

For a fixed mass of gas (the same amount, none let in or out) at constant temperature, pressure × volume always comes to the same fixed number: p × V = constant. p is the pressure in pascals (Pa) and V is the volume in cubic metres (m³).
Pressure and volume are inversely proportional: when one doubles, the other halves.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A gas has a pressure of 200 kPa and a volume of 3 m³. It is compressed to 1.5 m³ at the same temperature. What is its new pressure?
steps: Find p × V at the start: 200 × 3 = 600.
p × V stays the same, so afterwards p × 1.5 = 600.
Divide both sides by 1.5: p = 600 ÷ 1.5 = 400 kPa.

steps.text: You can also use kPa for the pressures and cm³ for the volumes, as long as the before and after values use the same units.

steps.question: Your turn. A gas at 100 kPa has a volume of 6 m³. It is compressed to 2 m³ at the same temperature. What is its new pressure, in kPa?

wrong.other: Not quite: 300 kPa. 100 × 6 = 600, so p × 2 = 600 and p = 300 kPa.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 300 kPa. It is pressure × volume that stays the same, not pressure ÷ volume: 100 × 6 = 600, so p = 600 ÷ 2 = 300 kPa.
wrong.times: Not quite: 300 kPa. 100 × 6 = 600; then divide by the new volume: p = 600 ÷ 2 = 300 kPa.

idk.hint: First find p × V at the start: 100 × 6. Then divide it by the new volume, 2.

steps.text: Here is a worked example of finding a volume. Its steps open one at a time.
steps.question: A gas at 100 kPa has a volume of 12 cm³. At the same temperature it is compressed until its pressure is 300 kPa. What is its new volume?
steps: Find p × V at the start: 100 × 12 = 1200.
p × V stays the same, so afterwards 300 × V = 1200.
Divide both sides by 300: V = 1200 ÷ 300 = 4 cm³.

steps.question: Air in a syringe is at 100 kPa with a volume of 30 cm³. At the same temperature it is pushed in until its pressure is 150 kPa. What is its new volume, in cm³?

wrong.wrongway: Not quite: 20 cm³. Higher pressure means a smaller volume: 100 × 30 = 3000, so V = 3000 ÷ 150 = 20 cm³.

idk.hint: Find p × V at the start: 100 × 30. Then divide by the new pressure, 150.

steps.question: A gas expands into a bigger volume at constant temperature. Which is true?

options.text: Its particles hit the walls less often

steps.right: Yes: with more space, the particles hit the walls less often, and the pressure falls. Their speed stays the same.

wrong.other: Not quite: its particles hit the walls less often.
wrong.slower: Not quite: the temperature is fixed, so their speed stays the same. With more space, they hit the walls less often.
wrong.bigger: Not quite: particles never change size. They spread further apart, so they hit the walls less often.

idk.hint: The temperature is fixed, so the speed is too. With more space, how often does each particle reach a wall?

steps.answerWhy: At constant temperature the speed stays the same; with more space the particles hit the walls less often, so the pressure falls.

steps.prompt: In one line: why does compressing a gas at constant temperature raise its pressure?
points: the particles have less space (closer together)
they hit the walls more often each second
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: in a smaller volume the particles hit the walls more often each second, so the pressure rises.

steps.text: Work done is the energy transferred when a force moves something. When you lift a bag, your force moves it and transfers energy to it: you do work on the bag.
A piston is a disc that slides along inside a tube, like the plunger of a bicycle pump. Push a piston into a gas and your force moves the piston, squashing the gas: you are doing work on the gas.
The energy from your push goes into the internal energy of the gas: the total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles.
In a gas nearly all of that is kinetic energy, so more internal energy means faster particles and a higher temperature.

steps.question: A diesel engine squashes air very quickly with a piston. Predict: which is true of the air's temperature?

options.text: It stays the same, as nothing heats it

steps.right: Yes: the piston does work on the air, raising its internal energy, so the air gets hot: hot enough to light the fuel.

wrong.falls: Not quite: the piston does work on the air, raising its internal energy, so its temperature rises.
wrong.same: Not quite: no flame is needed. The piston does work on the air, raising its internal energy, so its temperature rises.

idk.hint: The piston's force squashes the air. Does doing work on the air put energy in or take it out?

steps.answerWhy: The piston does work on the air, raising its internal energy and so its temperature.

steps.prompt: In one line: why does a bicycle pump get warm?
points: work is done on the air (the gas)
its internal energy rises, so its temperature rises
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: pushing the handle does work on the air, raising its internal energy, so its temperature rises.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: what causes gas pressure?
steps.right: Yes: particles colliding with the walls.

wrong.other: Not quite: particles colliding with the walls.
wrong.w1: Not quite: only collisions with the walls push on the container. Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls.
wrong.w2: Not quite: particles never change size. Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls.

steps.answerWhy: Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: a sealed jar of gas is cooled. Which is true of its pressure?
steps.right: Yes: slower particles hit the walls less often and less hard.

wrong.other: Not quite: it falls. Slower particles hit the walls less often and less hard.

steps.answerWhy: Cooling slows the particles, so they hit the walls less often and less hard: the pressure falls.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: a gas at 300 kPa and 2 m³ expands to 6 m³ at constant temperature. What is its new pressure, in kPa?
Quiz, question 4 of 6: a gas at 80 kPa and 20 cm³ is compressed to 5 cm³ at the same temperature. What is its new pressure, in kPa?
Quiz, question 5 of 6: a gas is compressed at constant temperature. Which is true of its particles' average speed?
steps.right: Yes: the temperature is fixed, so the speed is too.

wrong.other: Not quite: it stays the same, because the temperature is fixed.

steps.answerWhy: At constant temperature the average speed of the particles stays the same.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: why does pumping a tyre quickly warm the air in the pump?

options.text: Work is done on the air

steps.right: Yes: work done on the air raises its internal energy and its temperature.

wrong.other: Not quite: work is done on the air, raising its internal energy.
wrong.w1: Not quite: particles never change size. Work done on the air raises its internal energy, so its temperature rises.
wrong.w2: Not quite: warmer air has faster particles, not slower. Work done on the air raises its internal energy.

steps.answerWhy: Work done on the air raises its internal energy, so its temperature rises.
